[In an earlier post, I suggested Ted Kaczynski was a "mass murderer".
According to the definition criminologists use today to describe mass
murderers, this is grossly inaccurate.   A mass murderer is defined as a
person who kills two or more people in the same area over a very short
period of time.  Often, this is accomplished by the use of an explosive
device or firearm.  An example of a mass murderer is Timothy McVeigh.

Ted Kaczynski could be classified as a "serial killer".   A serial killer is
defined as a person who kills 2 (some say 3, but I don't see why it has to
be that way) or more people over an extended period of time, with "cool off"
periods between the murders.   Clearly, a serial killer must be more
scrupulous with his activities in order to avoid detection, so he can
continue getting his "job" done and simultaneously elude cature.

The main reason that I don't like to classify Ted as a serial killer is
because I don't believe he killed primarily for pleasure (which is the
motive for most serial killers).  I believe his killings were subserviant to
a greater cause -- to stimulate a revolution which he believed would bring
greater freedom for mankind or, at least, allow him to become a voice of
dissention that would be heard.

My use of the term "mass murderer" to describe him was, therefore, a very
poor euphemism.  Besides that, most serial killers are not nearly as bright
as Ted and have no likeable qualities in their character aside from the
ugliness that compels them to kill.   Hence, considering Ted's unique motive
for his killings, he should, in my opinion, be classified as a "terrorist".
And yes, I am showing a bias.]

Ph.D. Theodore Kaczynski wrote:

215. The anarchist [34] too seeks power, but he seeks it on an individual or
small-group basis; he wants individuals and small groups to be able to
control the circumstances of their own lives. He opposes technology because
it makes small groups dependent on large organizations.

Many have stated, or implied, that Ted is an anarchist.  It should be noted,
though, that he had no pretentions of being an anarchist.  In fact, he only
dedicated a very small paragraph in his Manifesto to describe the
motivations of an anarchist.   In addition, in the paragraph above in which
he describes anarchists he refers to them in third person.  While his
description of anarchists may resonate with how he feels, if he were an
anarchist he would have made it very clear from the beginning of his
Manifesto.  I think it would be fair to say that there are basic
psychological elements that he shares with anarchists.

As far as the various suggestions that Ted is a leftist is concerned, that
is preposterous. The rationalization behind this is the idea that his
criticism of leftism has been intended to be more constructive than
critical.  Again, this is wishful thinking; the intonation in his Manifesto
makes it very clear that he is, if anything, a right-winger who was
excoriating leftism.   That's not to say that he is a conservative, or even
a libertarian, as he was just as invective toward those who believe that
economic growth should be prioritized above everything else.
